core.p: Compare how soldiers are presented in **The Charge of the Light Brigade** and one other poem from the Conflict anthology. In your answer, you should consider the poets’ use of language, form and structure, and the influence of the contexts in which the poems were written. (20 marks)

bullets: Similarity: both show ordinary soldiers obeying a system they did not design; both use regular, song-like forms.
Difference: collective vs individual; glory vs guilt; distant narrator vs dramatic monologue; Crimean War vs Boer War.
core.p: Hinge: **reasoning**. Tennyson praises soldiers who do not ‘reason why’; Hardy, 48 years later, gives an ordinary soldier the chance to reason and shows him unable to find a reason.

bullets: **Thesis**: Tennyson presents soldiers as a noble collective whose value lies in unquestioning obedience; Hardy breaks the collective down to one man whose attempt to justify killing exposes war as senseless.
**P1 Identity**: ‘the six hundred’ vs ‘he and I’.
**P2 Obedience and reasoning**: ‘Theirs not to reason why’ vs ‘because —’.
**P3 Form**: galloping dactyls and refrain vs ballad quatrains broken by dashes.
**P4 Endings and context**: ‘Noble six hundred!’ vs ‘quaint and curious’; Laureate in 1854 vs Hardy in 1902.

essays.q: Compare how soldiers are presented in The Charge of the Light Brigade and one other poem.
essays.t: Model essay: The Charge of the Light Brigade and The Man He Killed
essays.text:
Tennyson presents soldiers as a noble collective whose glory lies in obeying without question, whereas Hardy isolates one soldier and allows him to question, only to reveal that the obedience Tennyson celebrates rests on no real reason at all.

Tennyson’s soldiers are never individuals. The refrain names them only as ‘the six hundred’, a collective noun that turns hundreds of men into a single heroic body moving ‘Into the valley of Death’. The biblical echo of Psalm 23 dignifies this movement, as if the men were pilgrims rather than casualties. Hardy deliberately reverses this perspective. His soldier speaks in the first person, and the opening line pairs him with his victim as equals: ‘Had he and I but met’. The conditional mood imagines a world of friendship in which the two would have shared ‘many a nipperkin’ at an inn, and the colloquial, dialect vocabulary marks the speaker as an ordinary working man. Where Tennyson’s soldiers are abstracted into a number, Hardy’s soldier and his enemy are two individuals who could have been friends.

The central difference is in how the poems treat thought. Tennyson admits that ‘Someone had blundered’, but the vague pronoun shields the officers, and the tricolon ‘Theirs not to make reply, / Theirs not to reason why, / Theirs but to do and die’ presents obedience as the soldiers’ honour; the alliteration of ‘do and die’ makes death sound as simple as an instruction. Hardy gives his soldier precisely what Tennyson’s lack: the chance to reason why. Yet when he tries, the line breaks: ‘I shot him dead because —’. The dash is the moment where the reason should appear, and nothing comes. He repeats ‘Because he was my foe’, and the over-insistent ‘Just so’ and ‘of course he was’ suggest someone trying to convince himself. Read beside Tennyson, Hardy’s poem seems to answer him: the soldiers who did not reason why might have found, like this speaker, that there was ‘No other reason why’.

Form reinforces these attitudes. Tennyson’s galloping dactyls (‘Half a league, half a league’) drive the poem forward with the confidence of a cavalry charge, and the mirrored stanzas three and five, with ‘in front of them’ changed to ‘behind them’, trace the ride down and back. Even the losses are expressed through the changing refrain, ‘Not the six hundred’, then ‘Left of six hundred’, so grief is controlled by the poem’s pattern. Hardy also uses a regular, ballad-like form of rhymed quatrains, but the regularity is disrupted from within. In the fourth stanza the dashes fragment the line ‘Off-hand like — just as I —’, mimicking hesitant speech, and the only enjambment across a stanza break, from ‘although’ into the next stanza, shows doubt literally spilling over the poem’s structure. Tennyson’s form stays in control; Hardy’s form shows a mind losing control.

The endings and contexts show why. Tennyson, as Poet Laureate writing weeks after Balaclava in 1854, ends with imperatives, ‘Honour the Light Brigade, / Noble six hundred!’, turning the poem into a public memorial that consoles a nation and reasserts Victorian values of duty. Hardy, writing in 1902 during the Boer War, when many volunteers were unemployed working men, ends with understatement: war is ‘quaint and curious’, because you shoot a man you would have treated in a bar or lent ‘half-a-crown’. The mildness of the adjectives is ironic; the speaker cannot express the horror directly. Ultimately, Tennyson asks his readers to honour soldiers for not thinking, while Hardy suggests that if soldiers were allowed to think, they would find the killing impossible to justify.
essays.thesis: Tennyson presents soldiers as a noble collective whose glory lies in obedience without question, whereas Hardy isolates a single soldier and lets him question, revealing that the obedience Tennyson celebrates rests on no real reason at all.
why: **AO2**: precise analysis of collective noun, allusion, conditional mood, dialect, tricolon, alliteration, dashes, metre, refrain, enjambment and understatement.
**Comparison**: the hinge (reasoning) organises every paragraph; Hardy is read as an answer to Tennyson.
**AO3**: Laureate and Victorian duty; Boer War volunteers, linked to specific choices.

model: Tennyson: anaphora of ‘Cannon to…’; shortest final stanza
Hardy: cyclical return to the inn; ABAB rhyme
exam.q: Practice: rewrite P3 (form) using a different pair of form features from each poem.
exam.tip: There are always more form features than you think: stanza length, rhyme, metre, refrain, punctuation.

mistakes.r: He admits a blunder but vaguely; the poem’s purpose is to honour.
mistakes.w: Saying Tennyson criticises the officers strongly.

mistakes.r: It was written in 1902 about the Boer War.
mistakes.w: Saying Hardy’s poem is about World War One.

summary: A full grade 9 model comparison of The Charge of the Light Brigade (named poem) and The Man He Killed, on how soldiers are presented; both poems are out of copyright, so the essay quotes freely as you should.

terms.d: Grammar for imagined situations (‘Had he and I but met’).
A noun for a group (‘the six hundred’).
